title: Ground Rent Seeking in US Economic History
existing_coverage: The wiki has extensive Foldvary coverage (people/fred-foldvary.md, research/foldvary-public-revenue.md, research/foldvary-kinetic-potential-rent.md, research/foldvary-business-cycle-synthesis.md, research/foldvary-reply-gochenour-caplan.md) plus separate pages on the specific 19th-century land-transfer episodes this paper surveys (concepts/railroad-land-grants.md, events/homestead-act.md, concepts/land-monopoly.md, concepts/government-granted-privileges.md, concepts/rent-seeking.md), but none of those pages summarize this specific paper or its public-choice framing of US land history as a whole.
reasoning: Fetched and read the full PDF text (SJSU seminar workshop paper, Sept 2014, by Fred Foldvary). It is a distinct, substantive piece: a public-choice history of US land-based rent-seeking from the colonial era (land speculation by Washington, Jefferson, Franklin et al.) through the Constitutional Convention, 19th-century land giveaways, and into a proposed structural voting reform to reduce rent-seeking — none of which duplicates the existing Foldvary pages (which cover the 1994 private-communities book, the 1997 business-cycle synthesis, and the kinetic/potential-rent framework, not this US-history/public-choice argument). It fills a real gap and follows the wiki's established one-page-per-major-Foldvary-paper pattern.
source_notes: Fred E. Foldvary, "Ground Rent Seeking in U.S. Economic History," seminar workshop paper, Economics Dept., San José State University, Sept. 19, 2014 (21 pp., unpublished/working-paper style, not peer-reviewed journal placement). Argues, via public-choice theory (Olson, Rowley), that US land policy from the colonial period through the 19th century was driven by concentrated-benefit/dispersed-cost rent-seeking over land and land rent (colonial land speculation by Founders, the Constitutional Convention's land-speculator interest group per Beard, the Proclamation of 1763, and westward land giveaways/grants), rooted in a mass-democracy structure unchanged since the Constitution, and concludes with a proposed alternative voting structure (small-group-based elections) to reduce the incentive for land-based rent transfers.

It does add value the existing page lacks: four practical preconditions for the theorem to hold in application (genuine service value, geographically bounded benefit, free-market rent-setting, mobile residents with uniform benefit/land ratios) plus two caveats (uneven benefit distribution across incomes, and hidden costs from reduced improvement values and displacement) that belong in a 'practical application limits' subsection.

Restates the theorem's condition (a public service can raise land rent enough to fund itself if collected as revenue) and lists four practical preconditions plus caveats about uneven benefit distribution and hidden costs (lower improvement values, displacement) that complicate real-world application.

title: Land Taxes: The Return of Henry George
existing_coverage: objections/lvt-not-enough-revenue.md already covers the revenue-sufficiency dispute in depth (Krugman, Blaug, various dollar estimates); people/milton-friedman.md already documents the 'least bad tax' quote; objections/lvt-is-socialism.md and objections/nationalization-solves-the-land-problem.md cover adjacent state-power concerns but not this piece's specific 'expropriation of current owners' + 'Leviathan/land-monopoly-by-government' framing.
reasoning: Fetched and confirmed: Pierre Lemieux, Econlib (Liberty Fund), Aug 17 2018 — a balanced secondary opinion piece, not primary research, that restates the standard efficiency/ethical case for LVT (citing Friedman's 'least bad tax' line, already on the wiki) but adds two citable figures/arguments not yet present: a concrete revenue-gap estimate (~$2.5T in all US land rent vs. ~$6T in government spending) and a distinct libertarian objection that state monopoly over land taxation risks a slow-motion 'Leviathan'/land nationalization, alongside a transition-fairness ('expropriation of current owners who bought on the assumption of future rent') objection. These are worth folding into the existing revenue-sufficiency objection page as an additional dollar estimate and a named critic, rather than a new page, since the core objection categories (revenue insufficiency, transition unfairness, state-power concentration) are each already covered elsewhere on the wiki.
source_notes: Pierre Lemieux, "Land Taxes: The Return of Henry George," Econlib (Liberty Fund), Aug 17 2018. Lays out the classical economic case for a land value tax (fixed supply, non-distortionary, fully capitalized into lower prices, 'least bad tax' per Friedman) and the ethical case (landowners did not create the rent public infrastructure generates), then raises three critical objections: a revenue-gap concern (all US land rent estimated at ~$2.5T/yr vs. ~$6T/yr in government spending, implying LVT alone can't fund current government), a transition-fairness concern (current owners bought land assuming no such tax — partial expropriation), and a state-power concern (a government monopoly on land taxation risks gradual land nationalization, a 'Leviathan').

title: How a development tool can increase property taxes
existing_coverage: concepts/land-value-capture.md lists tax increment financing (TIF) as one of six LVC instruments and separately carries a detailed San Antonio TIRZ case study on TIF's distributional problems; there is no dedicated TIF concept page and no existing coverage of Wisconsin's specific levy-limit interaction.
reasoning: Fetched and confirmed: Patrick McIlheran, Badger Institute (a Wisconsin free-market think tank), Aug 20 2026 — local policy journalism, not academic research, explaining a specific Wisconsin mechanism where TIF-district new construction counts toward a municipality's allowed levy increase but the added value doesn't count in the tax base used to spread that levy, mechanically raising the mill rate on everyone outside the TIF district. This is a genuine, narrow addition to the wiki's existing TIF material (which so far only has the San Antonio case) — a second, mechanically distinct way TIF can produce regressive side-effects — but is too state-specific and narrow (one policy quirk in one state) to support a standalone page; it strengthens the existing TIF discussion inside the land-value-capture page instead.
source_notes: Patrick McIlheran, "How a development tool can increase property taxes," Badger Institute, Aug 20 2026. Explains that under Wisconsin's municipal levy-limit law, new construction inside a Tax Increment Financing (TIF) district counts toward the 'net new construction' that lets a municipality raise its levy, but the TIF district's added assessed value is excluded from the tax base used to spread that levy across taxpayers — so opening or expanding a TIF district can mechanically raise the mill rate for everyone else. Notes TIF districts can run up to 27 years and cites a 647-acre Port Washington-area data-center TIF project as a live example.

title: Geo-Rent: A Plea to Public Economists
existing_coverage: Already cited (not as a dedicated page) in people/fred-foldvary.md (source #2, summarized in the 'Private provision of public goods' bullet) and research/foldvary-public-revenue.md (source #2, cited for the geo-rent revenue-share estimate) — but unlike Foldvary's other major papers (the 1994 book, the 1997 business-cycle synthesis, the kinetic/potential-rent columns, the Gochenour-Caplan reply), this specific 2005 EJW article has no dedicated research/ page of its own.
reasoning: Fetched and confirmed: Fred Foldvary, Econ Journal Watch 2(1), April 2005, pp. 106-132 — a real, notable, peer-reviewed-journal (open-access, editorially refereed) piece already treated as a primary source elsewhere on the wiki. It is currently under-served: cited twice as a secondary reference but never given the dedicated research-page treatment every other major Foldvary paper receives, meaning its full argument (public economics' systematic undervaluing of land rent, the claim that producer surplus is largely unrecognized land rent, and the concrete revenue-share estimate) is not fully exposed to readers via its own sourced page. This is a genuine, well-defined gap that follows the wiki's own established pattern.
source_notes: Fred E. Foldvary, "Geo-Rent: A Plea to Public Economists," Econ Journal Watch, Vol. 2, No. 1 (April 2005), pp. 106-132 (open access). Argues mainstream public economics has undervalued 'geo-rent' (the rental value of unimproved land) as a revenue base because it wrongly assumes land rent is a negligible share of national income and fails to recognize that much measured producer surplus is really land rent in disguise; invokes the Henry George Theorem as underused policy guidance and estimates geo-rent could fund a substantial share (by Foldvary's figure, roughly half) of all-level US government revenue, a figure the wiki's existing pages already flag as advocacy-dependent rather than consensus.
